title: Was Alaska Really Called Seward's Folly? #shorts
summary: Critics mocked the Alaska purchase, but most national periodicals of 1867 did not oppose it and the Senate approved the treaty 37 to 2.
tags: why did the us buy alaska
sources: "Russia has sold us a sucked orange!" proclaimed the New York World; the Senate approved the treaty for ratification by a vote of 37 to 2 (U.S. Senate Historical Office, Sumner's Alaskan Project): https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/treaties/sumners-alaskan-project.htm

Of the fifteen 'national' periodicals consulted, only three expressed an editorial opinion adverse to the purchase (Leslie's Weekly, the New York Nation, Harper's Weekly); the author calls mistaken the view that virtually only Seward did not think it a folly (Richard E. Welch Jr., 'American Public Opinion and the Purchase of Russian America', American Slavic and East European Review, 1958, peer-reviewed): https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-slavic-and-east-european-review/article/american-public-opinion-and-the-purchase-of-russian-america/97D5334491B23ACC840DA1A846405311

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html. The coral treaty lines are drawn approximately from the treaty's wording; the eastern line follows today's boundary.

scenes.narration: Everyone laughed at the Alaska deal and called it Seward's Folly. Right?
Critics did mock it. The New York World said Russia had sold us a sucked orange.
But historian Richard Welch checked {15|fifteen} national papers and magazines. Only {3|three} came out against it.

data.title: Mostly *on board*
data.source: R. E. Welch Jr., peer-reviewed study, 1958

scenes.narration: And the Senate approved the treaty {37|thirty-seven} to {2|two}.
So the jokes were real. They just weren't the whole story.
